speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But have we provided enough support to our hawkers who are the creators of that culture?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the question that prompted the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) to raise this Motion today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UNESCO accolade aside, hawker culture and hawker food are central to our Singaporean identity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawker centres, coffee shops and food courts are spaces for Singaporeans from all walks of life, rich or poor, regardless of race, language or religion, to interact and enjoy delicious, affordable food.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a true melting pot for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is one of the things that Singaporeans miss when they are overseas, myself included.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I was building my career overseas in 1990s, one of the things I missed most was a delicious bowl of laksa.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, I loved laksa so much that I had started a laksa stall in Tokyo in 2015 at the famous shopping district, Omotesando, in central Tokyo.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the hawkers who are behind the delicious local food that we enjoy have not been provided with sufficient support.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have a responsibility in this House to pass on our hawker culture to our future generations and to ensure that it not only survives, but flourishes, long into the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But our hawkers will need a lot of help and support at the national level to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to do more than putting up shows at the National Day Parade to celebrate our hawker food heritage.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many other ideas relating to building up the human capital of the industry and providing further support to hawkers have not been implemented.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also seek their indulgence to use some of their ideas in the debate today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Personally, the hawker trade is close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My late father was a hawker in Chinatown, the sole breadwinner for our family.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My sister is a wonton noodle hawker today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am deeply honoured to have the opportunity to speak up on this issue in this House today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP hopes that our Motion today will remind Singaporeans of the people behind the good and affordable food we enjoy every day.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these hawkers, advocates and supporters are with us in the House today, in the Strangers' Gallery, at my invitation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I will first discuss the importance of preserving and promoting our hawker culture before discussing the problems faced by hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Ms Hazel Poa and I will then put forward possible policies to resolve these problems.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These policy recommendations are based on the belief that the success of our hawker culture is inextricably tied to the success of our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, I will speak on the importance of preserving and promoting our hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP believes there are at least four major benefits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UNESCO recognition is an added reason for us to sustain this heritage.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The convenience and affordability of eating out also allowed many families to earn dual incomes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With millions of meals served to Singaporeans every day, hawker centres are the people's kitchens.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To maintain them, we have to first help our hawkers to survive and thrive.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, the hawker trade is one of the most conducive route for a budding entrepreneur to try out a business venture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I lived in Japan for many years, so I know of many Japanese who talked about starting a cooked food business as a business or hobby or just a place to meet friends and people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am beginning to see this among some of our younger Singaporeans today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But their dreams are often hindered by the high entry cost to the hawker business.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am confident that with lower rent and better working conditions, hawker centres can become incubators for our future food and beverage (F&B) entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last but not least, there are huge economic benefits if we promote our hawker food both domestically and internationally.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a parallel, Thai food has done very well globally.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thai dishes often rank among the top in global culinary surveys, overshadowing our local dishes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have been unhappy for a long time that chicken rice is recognised more as a Thai dish than a Singapore dish in Tokyo.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no reason why Singapore hawker food cannot be as world renowned as Thai food.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The well-reviewed Urban Hawker in New York, curated by Mr KF Seetoh, is an example of the success we can achieve if we do more as a nation to promote our hawker food overseas.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can extend our soft power by winning the hearts and minds of people all over the world through their stomachs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is another example of how we can punch above our weight.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, despite all the significant cultural and economic benefits that hawker culture can bring to us, it may wither in the future without policy adjustments to provide greater support to our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A serious examination of the problems faced by hawkers and new policies to address these problems are long overdue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The crux of the problem arguably is that the Government expects hawkers to provide cheap food as a safety net amidst the very high cost-of-living environment in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet at the same time, the Government has created a high-cost environment for hawkers to operate in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP calls for a holistic and comprehensive review of the hawker trade by the Government, which should cover all hawkers operating in hawker centres, coffee shops and food courts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will start by discussing the first problem of hawker centre management.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are more than 120 hawker centres in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Out of these, 12 are managed by private operators under the social enterprise model, as of 31 December 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the introduction of the social enterprise model in 2012, we have seen multiple conflicts between hawkers and social enterprise operators because of the high costs and onerous contractual conditions, compared to the National Environment Agency (NEA)-operated hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in 2018, the hawkers of the Jurong West Hawker Centre filed a petition against a 20-cent tray return surcharge imposed by Hawker Management, a social enterprise operator and subsidiary of the Koufu Group.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was also reported publicly in June 2024 that the hawkers of Bukit Canberra Hawker Centre tried to lower costs by asking the operator to let them use a cheaper gas provider, but they were denied.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawkers in social enterprise hawker centres also face many hidden costs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, they must bear the costs of offering loyalty discounts, budget meals and subscriptions to food delivery platforms.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All these are part of a long list of onerous contractual obligations on hawkers who may have to pay damages or receive demerit points if they fail to meet these requirements.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Following the outcry in 2018 against the social enterprise operators, NEA reviewed the key contractual terms between such operators and their stallholders and asked operators to make changes with effect from 1 January 2019.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the contractual terms seem to have continued to be very onerous, as I have confirmed in a contract signed by a hawker of a social enterprise hawker centre in 2022.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, the officeholders have repeatedly come out to say that the social enterprise model is sound, working well and has benefited hawkers and customers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is a sign that things are not going well when many more hawkers of social enterprise hawker centres are terminating their contract earlier, compared to hawkers of NEA-operated hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The social enterprise model is arguably not helping to sustain and grow the hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have done some calculations on the potential cost burdens imposed on hawkers by social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, it was reported that JW Heritage, another social enterprise operator and a subsidiary of the Chang Cheng Mee Wah Group, paid $4.86 million to the Government to manage the Jurong West Hawker Centre when it reopened in 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since there are 39 stalls there, this contract price translates into a cost of $125,000 per stall.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This cost represents a huge cost burden which must be recouped either from the stallholders or customers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But is it justifiable for private operators to extract surpluses or profits from hawker centres which are public assets, even if 50% is required to go back to programmes that benefit the hawker centres and hawkers?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will eliminate the problems in social enterprise hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP proposes that hawker centre management be taken over by a new Government agency tentatively called Hawker Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This agency can be formed by transferring the current Hawker Centres Group of NEA to it and then further expanding it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawker Singapore will oversee the management of all hawker centres in Singapore and the promotion of hawker culture domestically and internationally, working together with other relevant agencies, such as the Singapore Tourism Board and Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will work with hawkers in each hawker centre to develop its own unique value proposition within the general guidelines laid down by itself.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We envisage that Hawker Singapore will be advised by an independent industry expert panel to formulate strategies, finance expansion and assist hawkers to professionalise their business.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also propose that Hawker Singapore should set up a hawker academy to be a focal point for training young hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Former Member, Mr Leon Perera, had raised this in this House in 2021 and PSP supports this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A hawker academy will provide training and succession planning for hawkers, set standards for the hawker trade and help to preserve a selection of heritage foods that are important to our different communities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to centralising the management of all hawker centres, I will present three more policy recommendations to deal with the three other problems I discussed earlier.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These recommendations will provide the impetus to preserve and grow the hawker trade in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While rent may not be the biggest cost item for a hawker, it is the biggest burden because it is a fixed cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawkers can save on variable costs but not fixed costs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only the pioneer cooked food hawkers who were resettled from the streets get to enjoy subsidised rentals between $192 and $384 per month at the NEA-operated hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They represent about 30% of the hawkers today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The non-subsidised stalls which account for 70% of the hawkers must pay market rent determined via the tender system where stalls are rented out to the highest bidder.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While allowing bids to hit new records through the tender system, the Government also reduces a tendered rent to an assessed market rent when the hawker renews his contract after the initial three-year period.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, from the fourth year onwards, the $10,000 bidder will pay a much lower rent for the same stall.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last week, the Government announced that it would prolong the time required to adjust the tendered rent to the assessed market rent so as to deter excessively high hawker stall bids.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This latest change shows that the Government is aware of the problems of the current system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the question of why such a system still exists remains.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current tender system has the negative effect of driving up headline rentals in hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can have a ripple effect on the rents and values of Housing and Development Board (HDB) coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Several HDB coffee shops have been transacted at multi-million dollars in recent years bought by large business groups.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such high market prices for coffee shops have been a major cause of the rising cooked food prices and cost of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP recommends that we move away from the tendering model altogether.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, we propose a more flexible rent model, with the aim of lowering rent and curbing excessive speculation in coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, NEA has five categories of stalls: cooked food, halal cooked food, Indian cuisine, drinks and cut fruits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We suggest adding a sixth category, namely, heritage foods, to ensure that as many traditional foods unique to the different races in Singapore as possible are preserved.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, it would be nice to see a revival of Eurasian food in our hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Later, my colleague Ms Hazel Poa will present a possible model for curating hawker stalls.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP's proposed rental model is skewed to support smaller hawkers with lower rentals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will lower the barriers of entry for new hawkers and thus enhance the sustainability of our hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, it will not price out hawkers who are successful in growing their business.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The hawker trade is physically demanding, taxing on their health and even dangerous, especially for elderly hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, to serve the breakfast crowd at 6.00 am or 7.00 am, the hawkers must wake up at 1.00 am or 2.00 am.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Floors in hawker stalls are slippery or oily and hawkers must work around hot oil, knives and choppers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In September, it was reported that a famous Chinatown claypot rice hawker, Uncle Hong, decided to retire because of complications after he fell and broke his pelvic bone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Tan Hock Guan who ran the Michelin-recognised Guan Kee Fried Kway Teow stall in Ghim Moh also retired last November when he fainted while frying kway teow.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have witnessed, as a child, the many accidents and hardships experienced by the Chinatown neighbours of mine who are hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some might have made some money but, usually, they had to retire relatively young due to various ailments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For hawkers, additional manpower can help to reduce their workload and prolong their working life.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, apart from hawker stall owners, few Singaporeans would want to work at a hawker stall.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a completely new policy because the Government already allows companies operating coffee shops and food courts to hire Work Permit holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is difficult to understand why coffee shop and food court operators are allowed to employ Work Permit holders but individual hawkers are not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our policy proposal will not undermine the Singaporean character of our hawker centres because only one Work Permit holder is allowed per stall.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, our proposal will reduce the workload of senior hawkers and allow them to continue their trade for a longer time, while we encourage our younger Singaporeans and second-generation hawkers to enter the hawker trade with our new rent structure and training at the new hawker academy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This provides more assurance that our hawker culture remains sustainable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, to keep hawker food affordable in the immediate future, the Government should provide targeted discounts for needy groups and adjust the “budget meal” policies that have emerged in recent years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has introduced the “budget meal” initiative, possibly to insulate Singaporeans from rising costs in other areas like housing, Certificates of Entitlements and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The problem is, all these “budget meals” are paid by the hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawkers in social enterprise hawker centres are also forced to provide discounts, at their expense, to Pioneer, Merdeka and Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) cardholders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not believe there is any other industry where we contractually force suppliers to sell items below a certain price.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When HDB rents out shop spaces for supermarkets in the new estates, for example, HDB does not contractually force the supermarket operator to sell some budget food items below market prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why do we require this of our hawkers?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every cent earned by the hawkers is hard-earned money.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Half of the stallholders in the hawker centres are lower-income Singaporeans who received the Workfare Income Supplement in 2020.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These hawkers are in no position to do charity and should not be forced to do so.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawkers should be allowed to determine their own prices, which should not be controlled by the Government or operators.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They deserve to be fairly remunerated and incentivised to sell good and affordable food to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These discounts should be available for food at all hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can also provide lower-income households with more Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers so that they can use these vouchers to pay for their hawker meals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UNESCO accolade has given us an added reason to do so.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, high operating costs and harsh working environment have deterred younger Singaporeans from entering the hawker trade while existing hawkers are ageing and retiring.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, our distinctively Singaporean hawker culture and food are fast disappearing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government’s policy responses to these problems so far are too little and too late.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have shared four policy changes to improve the prospects and livelihoods of our hawkers so that they are motivated to professionalise, innovate and sustain our hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also propose a new rent model which will charge lower rent and is intended to have ripple effects on rents in coffeeshops and food courts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, we propose allowing each hawker stall to employ one Work Permit holder as stall assistant.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Ms Hazel Poa will speak on two other policy proposals later on centralising procurement of essential ingredients and revising the Code of Conduct for Leasing of Retail Premises.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that our six proposed policy changes will re-invigorate our hawker culture and allow it to shine brightly on the global culinary scene.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, it will ensure that the hawker centre, the people’s kitchen of our nation, will provide us with affordable food for many more generations to come.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only then can we say our hawker culture has truly lived up to its reputation as a UNESCO Intangible World Heritage.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans are extremely concerned about the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cost of food, including hawker food, is a big part of such concerns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For generations, hawker centres have been an essential place for working-class families to access delicious and affordable food in Singapore, and we should keep it that way.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To do that, not only do we need to keep the cost of hawker food under control, we also need to ensure that the overall hawker industry remains vibrant and being a hawker is a viable and sustainable livelihood for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why in our Motion statement today, we have emphasised that we must improve the prospects of hawkers so that we can sustain and grow our hawker culture and continue to enjoy good and affordable food.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The policies we propose today will improve the prospects and livelihoods of our hawkers and ensure that hawker food remains affordable for Singaporeans in the longer term.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Take for example our proposal of a fixed rental structure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, stalls are allocated to the highest bidders in tender exercises.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is generally held to be the economically efficient approach.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, PSP believes that the allocation of essential goods and services needs to account for other non-economic factors.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The subsidising of public housing, public transport and healthcare are examples of considering both social and economic factors in essential goods and services.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that this proposal will be a game-changer for hawkers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A reduction in rents in hawker centres will also have an anchoring effect on rents in privately-operated food courts and coffee shops.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If rent is not the mechanism used to allocate hawker stalls, how should they be allocated?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have said earlier that one way to do so is by random ballot.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another possible way is to allow the customers to decide.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, for hawker centres located near HDB flats, let the residents living nearby vote for their desired stalls through a small food fair or competition.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawker Singapore will ensure that the stalls that are chosen can still meet the needs of different ethnic groups.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that getting the stakeholders involved in the decision-making will lead to a more optimal outcome.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can first implement this on a trial basis at a few hawker centres to determine its feasibility before extending it to all hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can also provide lower-income households with more CDC Vouchers to pay for their hawker meals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will provide vulnerable groups with some much-needed assistance in the short term to ensure that their meals remain affordable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This approach ensures that assistance is more targeted at the more vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government’s current “budget meal” approach, however, is open to all.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past, we have argued for basic goods and services to be exempted from the Goods and Services Tax (GST).

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government’s response has always been that this would also benefit the rich, and targeted vouchers and rebates are better.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, I am sure the Government can understand how the hawkers feel when they see customers visibly better off than them financially, buying budget meals from them.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this not a case of double standards?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, our proposal is more sustainable because it will be funded by the Government instead of the hawkers themselves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawkers have the option to get their supplies through such arrangements or they could still choose to use their own suppliers if they think that it is of better quality or it gives them some other competitive advantage.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, we already have a company, ALPS Pte Ltd, that purchases drugs, medical and non-medical supplies and equipment, and services for Singapore’s three public healthcare clusters.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, PSP had called on the Government to centralise drug procurement across all public and private medical institutions and distribute drugs to public and private health facilities on a not-for-profit basis.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would not be a huge stretch to set up a similar centralised procurement system to bulk buy all the essential raw ingredients used by hawkers in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that such a system would have a very substantial impact on reducing the cost of living in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, the Government will not provide any subsidies to hawkers through this system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All savings will come from bulk purchasing the ingredients from wholesalers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have received feedback that, currently, some SEHC operators require hawkers to purchase supplies, such as gas and crockery from designated suppliers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has caused unhappiness in cases where the designated suppliers charged a higher price than free market.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that such provisions in the rental contracts are unfair to hawkers and provide potential for abuse and profiteering.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Landlords should not be specifying who their tenants should be buying from.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We propose that the Code of Conduct for Leasing of Retail Premises be revised to explicitly cover hawkers and prohibit all such practices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Contracts that deviate from this must seek the tenant's agreement and be submitted to the Fair Tenancy Industry Committee, as is the existing practice.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   For many years, hawker centres have played a crucial role in the lives of many Singaporeans, serving as places where we can obtain affordable food.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2020, hawker culture is inscribed onto UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To ensure that hawker culture can be preserved and continue to develop, PSP puts forward a Motion on hawker culture, calling on the Government to review its policies relating to hawkers and the management of hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is to address the various issues currently faced by hawkers, ensure that the industry can attract the next generation of Singaporeans and ensure that prices at hawker centres remain affordable for the public.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To improve the prospects and livelihoods of hawkers and to ensure that hawker centres can continue to provide affordable food, PSP today proposes six recommendations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to managing hawker centres nationwide, this agency will also be responsible for actively promoting hawker culture both domestically and internationally, in collaboration with other relevant agencies such as the Singapore Tourism Board and Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that under this rental model, most hawkers will pay lower rents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lowering rents at hawker centres will also help to reduce rents at private coffee shops and food courts, thereby lowering the cost of living for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If stalls are not allocated based on rent, how should they be allocated?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, Hawker Singapore could organise tasting sessions, inviting nearby residents to sample and vote to determine the winners of stalls in neighbourhood hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourth, in recent years, social enterprise hawker centres and HDB-leased coffee shops have successively mandated hawkers to provide "budget meals" at their own cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP does not oppose budget meals, but we believe they should be funded by the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many hawkers do not earn high incomes and they work hard for their money.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They should not be forced to provide budget meals at their own cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe a better approach would be for the Government to pay for targeted discounts or meal vouchers for those in need.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help lower the prices of cooked food, thereby reducing the cost of living for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sixth, PSP has received feedback that some operators of social enterprise hawker centres currently require hawkers to purchase gas and crockery from designated suppliers at higher prices, causing unhappiness.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe such provisions are unfair to hawkers and could potentially be abused for profiteering.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We suggest amending the Code of Conduct for Leases of Retail Premises to prohibit such practices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that the six proposals we put forward today will effectively lower the cost of living for Singaporeans and strengthen the sustainability of our hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope the Government will seriously consider implementing the recommendations we have proposed today. : Mr Speaker, Sir, PSP understands that many Singaporeans, especially the lower income and the elderly are extremely concerned about the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, affordable hawker food has been one of the major ways through which the cost of living has been kept in check for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As circumstances change, we need to adjust our policies to ensure that hawker food remains affordable in a sustainable way.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that our six proposals will substantially help lower the cost of living for Singaporeans while ensuring that being a hawker remains a viable and sustainable livelihood for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that the Government will seriously consider these proposals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These acknowledgments are testimony to the success of the Government's approach because our beloved hawker centres and the special role that they play in Singaporean life is a result of the People's Action Party (PAP) Government's policies and support over the years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From the early years when roving hawkers were brought into centres built specially for them and supported, the expansion of hawker centres into the heartlands, the Hawker Upgrading programmes and so on; evolving over time until they have become treasured institutions that they are today, even to the extent of achieving UNESCO Cultural Heritage status and being much in demand in our new housing estates.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have a very special place in our Singapore psyche, having filled our tummies over the years with warm familiar foods and our hearts with much warmth and comfort.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe every Singaporean has a lovely, bittersweet, maybe even milestone defining, memory tied to our hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps a first date over rojak, a serious sibling discussion over claypot rice, a "lao di fang" Tiger beer hangout spot with friends.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Singaporean lives are intertwined with the safe spaces offered by hawker centres and, of course, by the familiar faces of our favourite hawker uncles and aunties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this was not always the case in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It may seem inconceivable to many, but what we recognise as hawker centres today, did not exist until the 1970s.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, hawker centres are a fairly new construct.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Prior to hawker centres, our hawkers existed in our community as street vendors.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was not too long ago that street hawkering was still seen as a public disamenity and this is still a Singaporean living memory.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recall that, as a child, my uncle telling me one evening that he was unsuccessful in procuring his satay at Glutton's Square as the street hawkers had fled, in front of him, from special squads of illegal hawker inspectors.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Even with these changes, throughout the years, one thing remains constant – our hawkers never had it easy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the early years, our street hawkers made their living in extremely difficult conditions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, as times changed, even after the establishment of hawker centres, hawkers still needed to work long hours, starting early and finishing late, to fulfil their commitment to the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just think about it – that is a workload of 18 hours a day, six days a week.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our hawkers soldier on because they are committed to serving our community and the residents in our estates.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our hawkers are proud of the hawker trade and it is because of this that Singapore's hawker culture has been listed in UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hawkers affect the lives of Singaporeans in many ways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You have touched our lives and shaped our Singaporean way of life with your care, and your legacy will be carried on for many generations. : Mr Speaker, many hawkers toil day in and day out with the repetitive work of a hawker, such as frying hundreds of plates of, say, char kway teow, a day to just give us more wok hei.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has caused our hawkers back and hand injuries, sometimes even permanently damaging their nerves.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our hawkers experience bar rot, which is an itchy, painful hand fungal infection due to wet work surroundings, washing produce and cleaning our utensils.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our hawkers soldier on because they are committed to serving our community and the residents in our estates.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our hawkers are proud of the hawker trade and it is because of this and their hard work that Singapore is now a UNESCO site for cultural heritage.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To this, I thank our many hawker brothers and sisters in the gallery for accepting our PAP Members' invitation to be here with us today.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And to all our hawkers and friends listening in, watching this Parliamentary debate: your resilience, your care and your dedication to our community, Singapore thanks you.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You have touched our lives and you have shaped our Singaporean way and know that your legacy will continue to touch our lives to many, many generations to come.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Looking ahead, I think we can all agree that we must see how we can continue to support our hawkers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As consumer preferences, workforce demographics and business models evolve, so must our hawkers and the hawker trade.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to keep a steely eye on the win-win national desires of providing affordable food for Singaporeans, with supporting the lives and livelihoods of our hawkers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For hawkers, business costs stem mainly from raw materials, manpower, utilities, rentals, platform delivery fees and shared services, like dish washing and tabletop cleaning.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over at the Labour Movement, we are keeping an eye on ensuring that Progressive Wage Model moves in the cleaning and food services industries are fairly shared amongst stakeholders as uplifting lower-wage workers are a whole-of-community effort.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our hawkers, being at the frontline to keep daily meals affordable, are often caught in budget meal crossfires and are sometimes left holding the ground on budget meal prices, unsure of where to look for wider community support.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In speaking with hawker centre and food court operators, like NTUC Foodfare, I note that budget meal innovations have been introduced.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, the Rice Garden by Fairprice Group Initiative by Foodfare provides budget meals to CHAS and COMCare card holders, with prices controlled by Foodfare.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other local initiatives, like our CDC Vouchers and Punggol Shore's Care Voucher Programme works hand in hand with stall operators in providing for the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a nation, we have continued to keep a very watchful eye on this win-win national desire, even as we continue building up, adding to and innovating the rich hawker culture we have.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the constant reviewing and taking in feedback from hawkers and stakeholders ensure that our hawker culture continues to hit home right.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Wei Siang shares that this eats into the already slim profit margins of his sweet glutinous rice ball soup and, as such, he has to sometimes charge patrons extra when they request for more bowls.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has led to some very unkind comments in his Google reviews.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yes, I did read up on the reviews and these are what some of the public comments are: "Would not recommend.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The seller was quite unreasonable and trying to overcharge an additional bowl", one out of five stars for service review; "Bad attitude!

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Spend your money somewhere else", one out of five stars overall review.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Wei Siang was obviously upset and hurt with these reviews, and I can understand why.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I am also glad to note that there are progressive and supportive stakeholders too.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I spoke with several cleaning and dishwashing service providers and found out that they, too, understand the difficulties faced by our hawkers and have, on their own accord, created programmes to support our hawkers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the years, we have seen many happy outcomes from running a hawker business.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My friend Valerie and her brothers, Adrian and Pathom, who are up in the gallery today, are fourth generation owners of Xi De Li.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Their great-grandparents fried you char kway as street hawkers in the 1920s.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Valerie tells me that she is thinking about venturing overseas and has innovative product development plans, such as making a Singapore-version of churros from you char kway.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the Labour Movement is now assisting her in her optech roadmap and the use of technology to upskill her workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like Valerie's parents, grandparents and great-grandparents before her, many of our hawkers have done well for themselves and passed on their legacies to their families.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of their children choose to leave the family trade and pursue interests in the arts, law and engineering, others like Valerie and her brothers have chosen to stay and to continue as pillars in this industry.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Valerie is in good company, very good company.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She is part of Food Gen 2 (食二代), which is a grouping of second-generation F&B owners and some running companies spanning over five generations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are a very strong, close group of 100 members, making positive strides on the ground towards a sustainable and strong future for F&B and our hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are here in the gallery today to lend support to our hawkers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our current dynamic hawker landscape is a result of the hard work and dedication of hawkers, as well as many policy reviews and innovations by the Government working with the community over the years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I wholeheartedly agree that we should continue to review our policies relating to hawkers and hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But at the same time, to be fair, we should also recognise that much have been done over the years, in terms of policy and support and this is a continuing journey.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Defending Singapore's hawker culture and hawkerpreneurs's livelihood is a deeply personal matter to me as I have experienced first-hand the grit, determination and passion of our hawkerpreneurs and have close friends in the ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, I have personally experienced several reviews that led to tangible improvements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our hawkerpreneurs are everyday heroes who toil over their hot stoves to provide all of us with affordable and tasty meals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From my direct engagement with hawkerpreneurs, it is clear that the two largest cost drivers are the cost of raw ingredients and manpower, not rent, as is commonly perceived and acknowledged by Member Mr Leong Mun Wai as well.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means for every serving of hawker meal we order for $4, $2 to $2.40 is paid to ingredients suppliers, 60 cents to $1 for manpower and 40 cents is paid for rental.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are other miscellaneous expenses, such as transport and utilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This breakdown highlights the thin profit margins and underscores the importance of addressing the need of our hawkerpreneurs to earn a decent livelihood.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To illustrate the challenges with ingredient costs on the ground, allow me to share about Mr Zuhairi, who runs Project Penyek at Senja Hawker Centre.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Zuhairi shared that customer preferences for certain parts, such as thighs over breast meat, lead to imbalances and wastage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unsold breast meat at the end of the day has to be discarded, increasing the cost of goods sold significantly.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He mentioned, "When customers ask for more thighs, I worry about the breast meat that may go unsold.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Any wastages directly affects my earnings." These days when I order Ayam Penyet at his stall, Mr Zuhairi will jokingly ask me "Breast or thigh?" I will obviously reply "Chicken breast".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Zuhairi orders chilli to make tasty sambal that goes perfectly well with his Ayam Penyet.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But Mr Zuhairi expressed anxiety over customers requesting extra sambal chilli sauce, which they expect at no additional charge.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With margins already slim, such additional requests further strain finances.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He shared, "I want to satisfy my customers, but giving more chilli without charging increases my ingredients cost." Mr Speaker, these anecdotes may seem trivial to some, but I felt that it is important to share the ground concerns and anxieties of our hawkerpreneurs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are issues we may not think of as consumers when we buy our food.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thankfully, Mr Zuhairi shared that ingredients prices have stabilised.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This signals that the monetary measures, such as strengthening the Singapore dollar put in place by the Government, have helped.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With regard to Member Ms Hazel Poa's suggestion on centralised procurement at hawker centres, I would like to share that operators have explored these ideas, but certain challenges make it difficult to implement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, hawkerpreneurs' ingredients are highly varied, with many different stock keeping units.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, even something as simple and common as rice, comes in various types and grades, complicating central procurement and bulk purchasing efforts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, many hawkerpreneurs have longstanding relationships with their suppliers and prefer to maintain these trusted connections.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another key challenge that hawkerpreneurs face is the cost and lack of manpower.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As part of our national commitment to uplift lower-wage workers, manpower costs have increased.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Local jobseekers are also needed in other sectors, such as childcare and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recognising these challenges, during one of my catchups with hawkerpreneur friends – one of whom is Mr Noorman Mubarak, founder of Nasi Lemak Taliwang – they suggested allowing them to hire Long-Term Visit Pass Plus (LTVP+) holders to alleviate the manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I felt that this was a good suggestion, as LTVP+ holders are part of the Singaporean family.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allowing hawkers to hire LTVP+ holders will balance both the need for an additional pool of workers to hire, mitigate concerns that our hawker centres should be distinctively Singaporean and provide additional job options for Singaporean families.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As shared earlier, this policy change not only provides hawkers with an additional pool of manpower, but also increases job opportunities for LTVP+ holders, who are often family members of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I note that some hawkerpreneurs have asked to be allowed to hire foreigners on Work Permits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are mindful of community concerns about allowing more foreigners to work in hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hansard records from 2010 and 2011 reflect concerns over the influx of foreign workers in hawker centres, with residents noting issues, such as language barriers, cultural differences and variations in service standards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the Parliamentary Sitting on 1 March 2010, then-Minister for the Environment and Water Resources, Dr Yaacob Ibrahim, acknowledged these concerns, "Some Members have raised concerns about the increasing presence of foreign workers in hawker centres, which may affect the ambience and character of these places.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also concerns about communication difficulties and differences in hygiene practices." It is important to acknowledge these concerns and strive for a balance between addressing manpower needs and preserving the authenticity of our hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Next, I would like to speak about the management model of hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The SCHC model has been subject to much discussion in the past and in today's debate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is essential to share some sentiments of hawkerpreneurs presently.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One that I know very well is the Senja Hawker Centre in Zhenghua.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a new hawker centre managed under the SCHC model.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The FairPrice Group is the appointed management company by NEA.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: She needed guidance to navigate various licensing matters, such as understanding which licenses were necessary and figuring out how to set up a utility account.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employment laws and finding reliable supplier contacts were also obstacles along the way.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The centre manager from the SCHC operator became a vital source of support, helping her through each requirement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In her own words, she shared, "Without the support of the centre manager, I would have felt lost and it would have taken me much longer to start my business." Such support is invaluable, especially for the next generation of hawkerpreneurs, who may not have the industry knowledge and networks that veteran hawkerprenurs have built over the years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the guidance of dedicated centre managers, new hawkerprenuers like Angeline are better positioned to navigate these challenges and build successful businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SCHC operators also assist in procuring shared services, such as centralised dishwashing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has significantly alleviated manpower challenges as they are not required to wash dishes themselves.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The dishes are cleaned by a third-party vendor.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hawkers at Senja Hawker Centre expressed satisfaction with these services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Yeo, a senior hawker who owns Yong Feng Ji Chicken Rice, shared that centralised dishwashing saves them time and allows them to focus on cooking and serving their customers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While SCHC has brought clear value to most hawkers, some have also provided feedback on areas of concern with the SCHC model.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, the operational hours minimum requirements can be rigid, making it challenging for a single-operator stall to comply.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It gets harder to comply when hawkers face manpower challenges and need time for personal exigencies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other hand, the minimum operating hours requirement is to ensure that there are sufficient choices for patrons and minimum vibrancy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is challenging for the management to attract footfall to a centre if there are insufficient stalls open for business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that a genuine solution is to find a realistic fit somewhere between these two expectations and every single hawker centre will be different due to local community needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of perceiving the SCHC model as the boogeyman, we need to solve the real challenge: how do we fine-tune the model to meet the needs of our hawkerpreneurs and the communities they serve?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Taking a leaf from PAP's tripartism, we can extend hawkerpreneurs' representation under the SCHC model to a similar model to that of existing hawkers' and merchants' associations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This provides an opportunity for collective feedback from hawkerpreneurs to SCHC operators and NEA to co-create industry standards around contractual matters and ground issues that align hawkerpreneurs with local needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The SCHC model definitely has value and it is the hawkerpreneurs informing us about how things are better for them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us work together with the operators and hawkerpreneurs to make continuous improvements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rising costs of ingredients and manpower costs continue to erode their already slim profit margins, leaving little for their own livelihood.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our hawkerpreneurs provide incredible societal value by offering affordable food to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To truly appreciate the affordability of our hawker food, let us compare it to street food prices in other major cities around the world, relative to the median incomes in those cities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, a meal accounts for around 0.26% of the median income.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moving to Hong Kong, the median monthly wage is about $3,378 and a simple street meal can cost around $8.50, making up about 0.25% of the median income.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even in Western cities like New York City, where the median monthly wage is about $6,626, the cost of a basic meal represents a larger proportion of the median income compared to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In New York, a street meal costs around $13.00 and takes up about 0.2% of the median income.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Earlier, Mr Leong Mun Wai referred to the hawker stalls at Urban Hawker in New York, curated by Mr KF Seetoh.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Mothership article also reported that hawkerpreneurs in New York cited high rental, ingredients and manpower costs and other challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sadly, at least one hawkerpreneur has closed since.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was told that more have closed in recent months.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But yet our local hawker centres are still able to provide us with affordable meals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am aware and empathise with residents who think of affordability based on what they used to pay, rather than what others in other countries have to pay.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, such economic data points across cities provide a clear reality of our comparative situation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding this, our hawkers provide high-quality, diverse and delicious meals at prices that are a fraction of what people pay in other global cities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This affordability is Singapore's unique social compact forged out of a vocation to feed the nation, but it also underscores the financial pressures hawkers face.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we reflect on Singapore's social compact, let us also take a moment to consider how each of us can contribute to helping our hawkerpreneurs earn a fair and sustainable livelihood.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hawkers have expressed that while customers are willing to pay $15 for a bowl of ramen, they hesitate to pay $5 for a handmade bowl of fishball noodles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that as a deeper appreciation of our hawkerpreneurs grows, the consumer will respond to pricing favourably because they know and understand what it takes to deliver good hawker food.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must support them to ensure they can continue this vital service without compromising their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the Government's side, one particular initiative that has balanced affordability with accessibility well is the Government's CDC Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The CDC Vouchers have directly provided Singaporean households with more to spend at the hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hawkerpreneurs at Senja Hawker Centre shared that the vouchers not only increased their sales but also introduced new customers to their stalls.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a recent catch-up with Mr Melvin Chew, who is the founder of Hawker United Dabao 2020 Facebook group that has more than 330,000 members and also the owner of Jin Ji Teochew Braised Duck and Kway Chap – and I understand he is here today and I want to acknowledge his presence – which is located at Chinatown Complex Market and Food Centre, he shared candidly that the CDC Vouchers have been extremely helpful for the patrons in Chinatown as many are seniors who have retired.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He has witnessed seniors holding stacks of CDC Vouchers as well-wishers donate CDC Vouchers to them and seniors can now gather to enjoy a nice tze char meal instead of being restricted to just budget items.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also many notable examples of Pay It Forward initiatives in hawker centres around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This example shows that Singaporeans can align local initiatives to show their support for those with less.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that we can provide more CDC Vouchers to resource low-income families and our seniors who are mostly retired.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Providing additional vouchers to them ensures they continue access to affordable meals and it supports hawkers by increasing patronage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Zhenghua, we have also introduced $1 deals as part of our local initiatives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These deals were fully sold out in three days.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My grassroots team and I are now exploring ways to expand this initiative so that even more hawkers and residents can benefit.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Corporations can also play a significant role in supporting our hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The scheme encourages users to dine at hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These programmes underscore that much has been done to support our hawkerprenuers and ensure that food remains affordable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It takes a whole-of-society approach to support our hawkerpreneurs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From Government policies to corporate initiatives and consumer's attitudes, everyone has a role to play in sustaining this vital part of our culture.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, Mr Speaker, Sir, with your permission, may I propose amendments to the Motion?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of your proposed amendments?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The proposed amendments submitted by the Member are in order.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do you have copies available for other Members?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will give some time for the copies to be distributed before you move your amendments.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Chia, I have also frozen the time clock.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is not eating into your speech time, although you are getting close to the 20 minutes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Alright, I think all Members have received a copy of your amendments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, "In line 2, to delete the words ‘to provide better support for hawkers’ and insert ‘which will help’".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And third, "At the end of line 3, to add ‘while enabling hawkers to earn a fair livelihood’".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can proceed with the rest of your speech.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: They are places where we connect, share and celebrate our diverse heritage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Let us work together – the Government, businesses and citizens alike – to ensure that our hawkerpreneurs can make a fair livelihood and that everyone can enjoy affordable food.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It may be convenient that the debate on the original Motion and on any other amendments moved by Members be proceeded with simultaneously as a debate on a single question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement to this?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our hawker centres are deeply ingrained in our cultural identity and our collective memories, and these familiar communal spaces and their associated sights, smells and tastes are what make Singapore feel like home for many of us.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just ask anyone who has been abroad for even just a week.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are also passionately protective of our hawker food culture, to the extent that there is always some healthy debate among Singaporeans about which hawker stall serves the best Hokkien mee or, for that matter, some friendly rivalry with our friends across the Causeway about whether the Kuala Lumpur-style Hokkien mee with its thick egg noodles stir fried with black soy sauce is superior or the Singapore-style Hokkien mee with a mixture of yellow wheat noodles and bee hoon braised in prawn stock.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, there could be little left to protect, with our hawker food culture at risk of eroding rapidly, and the sustainability and very existence of our hawkers under threat, if we do not take proactive steps to fix the current issues at hand and remodel the way our hawker trade is managed today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On that note, Mr Speaker, while I had initially wanted to raise a similar matter in an Adjournment Motion, I will still cover the same points in my speech today on three broad areas: addressing the business costs for hawkers, addressing the cost of living for Singaporeans and, lastly, on revitalising the industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The very existence of our hawkers hinges on whether it is sustainable for the hawkers to ply their trade and operate a financially viable business.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In recent years, there has been no lack of news about F&B operators closing, even some high-profile hawkers whom many find surprising, given their popularity with patrons.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A recent example is Zhong Xing Foochow Fish Balls and Lor Mee in Bukit Merah, where the owners lamented that they had to close their 82-year-old family-run business, due to their old age, an impending doubling in rent and unwillingness to pass on higher prices to their regular customers, many of whom are the elderly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Caught between rising costs and the difficulty or even reluctance in raising prices, many hawkers are simply finding it difficult to sustain a decent livelihood.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Addressing the business costs for hawkers is thus a key thrust of my speech today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our conversations with hawkers suggest that rentals and their associated costs for raw materials and manpower are the key costs for running their businesses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, it is important to point out that while the cost of ingredients is a key variable cost for our hawkers, rentals represent a key overhead cost that imposes a high hurdle that hawkers have to overcome on a monthly basis, before they can even start to make a profit, leading many to feel as though they are working for the landlord for a long time before working for themselves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And the cycle repeats every month, with many hesitant to take a long break as a result.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, rentals are a key cost component that we can influence and try to control, as opposed to raw material costs which are primarily dependent on global commodity price trends and may not be directly under the Government’s control.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we see that even for the largest listed F&B companies in Singapore, their pre-tax margins hover between a low single digit margin and even losses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, for our hawkers operating at a much smaller scale, every single percentage point counts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Whether rentals represent 10% or 20% of operating costs, bringing rentals down by even a few percentage points from their total operating costs could mean the difference between shutting down or not.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is where I believe we can easily do more to better support our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my speech during the Committee of Supply debates earlier this year, I was comforted to hear that there was a rental cap for this year’s Geylang Serai Ramadan Bazaar, similar to that in 2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To quote the Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development Faishal Ibrahim: "We hear you.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For Bazaar Raya Geylang Serai 2024, we are taking steps to ensure that it is more affordable for our sellers and consumers".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Whether it is the F&B stalls at the bazaar or at our hawker centres, I believe the affordability concerns remain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Could we not adopt the same rental cap idea for our NEA-operated hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Whether or not the particular stall passes on the higher costs, which I believe is only logical, is just one aspect of the problem.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The other aspect is that if such a trend continues, this will have knock-on effects on the supposed market rate as determined by an independent professional valuation, leading to higher market rents and an upward spiral for other hawkers if this persists as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, HDB is already evaluating the tenders for eating houses under the price-quality method.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why can we not do the same for our hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If it is implementation challenges that NEA is concerned about, I would suggest that they work with the HDB commercial teams to understand how this is being done for what is essentially the same trade.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A hawker whom I spoke to, who is very supportive of the PQM method, also suggested some factors for the NEA’s consideration, such as the pricing of their products, operating hours, whether they are young hawker entrepreneurs and the heritage value of the product, to begin with.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wish to reiterate a point raised in the Workers’ Party 2020 manifesto, which called on all hawker centres to eventually be brought under NEA control, as that would provide the necessary long-term assurance to hawkers that there are governmental levers of control over rents, not only today, but also tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The ultimate goal of an SEHC is to make a profit and not provide a public good.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, hawkers are often at the behest of their SEHC operators.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With operators having access to point of sales (POS) data, these operators are incentivised to maximise the rentals and occupancy costs of their hawkers, which, while in the best financial interest of the SEHC operator, may not be in the interest of the hawkers and ultimately consumers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such an environment will also not be conducive to creative budding entrepreneurs, but favour established chains with scale, and the lack of diversification of our hawker food mix may even be a consequence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having all hawker centres under the common management of the NEA also creates consistency in criteria, standards and policies for all hawkers to follow.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, I am not painting all SEHC operators with the same broad brush.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But there are certainly some questionable practices of certain operators which require urgent attention today, even if plans for the centralised management of SEHCs are not implemented immediately.
