speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are consumers and hawkers benefiting from some of these onerous terms?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Government to regularly review the contractual terms and conditions between the SEHC operators and stallholders to better protect the welfare and interests of our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Next, I move on to addressing the cost of living for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Short of stating the obvious, we all need to eat and it is a matter of sustenance and survival.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe the public do understand and appreciate that running a hawker stall entails rising overhead costs, along with other intangible factors, such as long preparation hours, the years of honing and refining their recipe and craft, and the hot and sweaty work environment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our hawkers are trapped between a rock and a hard place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On one hand, they must contend with price hikes in raw ingredients and utilities, coupled with high rentals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the other hand, seeing how price increases could potentially turn away customers whilst worsening the financial burden experienced by low-income patrons, many stall owners are hesitant about raising their prices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Now, with the requirement to sell their budget meals at a Government-mandated “budget” price at the expense of their already-dwindling incomes, hawkers ultimately bear the biggest brunt of the budget meal scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As lamented by a hawker interviewed by The Straits Times in an article dated 1 June 2024: “It is impossible to make a profit from these meals”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In an attempt to maintain their livelihoods, several hawkers have turned to other methods to cover costs from their budget meals, often at the expense of the meal’s quality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, there have been instances of budget meals with small portion sizes, while several have also noticed nutritionally imbalanced budget meal offerings with heaps of carbohydrates coupled with little to no proteins.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our hawkers, many of whom are sole proprietors, should not have the Herculean task of shouldering the burden of providing Singaporeans with “cheap” meals to cope with the cost of living crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, they should have the freedom of setting their own prices, given that they have an astute understanding of their business costs and the need to sustain their livelihoods, whilst keeping it affordable enough to ensure a steady flow of customers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of mandating the menu prices that hawkers should set and having our hawkers shoulder the burden of addressing food costs, the Government ought to do more to ensure the affordability of hawker food, given that it has the capacity and resources to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, several residents have experienced difficulties when obtaining these vouchers, such as those who are living in another house from the one stated on their National Registration Identity Card, those living in shelters and those who face strained familial ties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Aside from providing some relief to the cardholder’s medical bills, this scheme is already being used in supermarkets, such as FairPrice, to provide discounts to cardholders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, cardholders who present their CHAS card at a participating hawker would be able to receive a discount on their food.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Whether it is blue, orange or green, the quantum of discount would then correspond to these different levels.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, the cost of these discounts should not be imposed on the hawkers, but on the Government instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than subsidise high net worth individuals or millionaires who, like low-income households, all receive CDC Vouchers, the subsidy would be better directed to those who need them the most.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such a move would help to minimise the administrative and operational costs in providing affordable meals by tapping on the infrastructure and systems of a pre-existing scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, it would help to improve access to those who experience difficulties in obtaining and redeeming their CDC Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By enhancing governmental support to ensure affordable meals whilst securing the livelihoods of our hawkers, younger players could come in and rejuvenate the hawker scene, whilst bucking the trend of a rising number of veteran hawkers opting to call it quits and retire.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Another means for hawkers to broaden their reach is by listing their business on food delivery platforms such as Foodpanda, GrabFood and Deliveroo.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such platforms have also provided many of our residents, tired after a long day at work, easy access to tasty and delectable food right at their doorstep.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially prevalent in estates such as Sengkang, where many residents have turned to food delivery platforms due to the lack of coffee shops and hawker centres in the area.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the hefty platform fees incurred by merchants on food delivery platforms have resulted in them either increasing their menu prices accordingly or opting to absorb it into their menu prices, which results in a decrease in profits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In a PQ filed in 2021, Minister for Trade and Industry Mr Gan Kim Yong outlined that the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS) will continue to monitor the food delivery sector for any anti-competitive practices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of adopting a heavy-handed approach to managing hawkers and the prices they charge, perhaps the food delivery platforms, who are in a financially stronger position, could be the ones subject to greater oversight by the Government instead, especially with regard to the platform fees, which are hefty relative to food value.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Fee transparency is a key measure to ensure that competition can truly yield a fair platform fee for all hawkers and F&B operators and level the playing field between sole-proprietor hawkers and large restaurant chains in dealing with these delivery platforms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such a measure also helps customers understand the true costs of delivery and protect hawkers from hidden fees and charges.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate the CCCS had issued interim measures directions during the possible acquisition by Grab of Delivery Hero's business in Singapore, which did not ultimately materialise eventually, would the Government consider such measures to help ameliorate the cost borne by merchants for their presence on such platforms?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Certainly, with greater oversight of the food delivery business, food establishments, especially our hawkers, could be provided with another means to grow their business and thrive, while providing consumers with another affordable dining option.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When I say "revitalisation", I mean it literally in that there is a decline that needs to be reversed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Too many indicators suggest that the industry is in trouble, not just financially as I have mentioned earlier, but also culturally.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This retirement of a whole generation of hawkers is also evident in the disappearance of certain Singaporean dishes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Kueh tutu, appam, satay bee hoon and Fujian oyster cakes are increasingly rare and almost unheard of in new hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Food historian Khir Johari, in his book "The Food of Singapore Malays", talks about dishes that have already disappeared, such as mee maidin and rujak su'un.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just as critically, he notes how corners are cut and old recipes are disregarded in Singaporean food culture.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to recognise that the Hawkers' Development Programme and Hawkers Succession Scheme do not work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do not know of any other way to describe this, but we need to go back to the drawing board and examine the reasons for this and re-model the existing schemes which are no longer fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the role of hawker food in our economy may not change so quickly because the demand for low-cost food is always there, its role in our culture is undisputed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must make sure we protect it for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2020, UNESCO decided to inscribe our hawker culture on its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In our sub mission, it was highlighted several times that efforts are being made to pass on culinary practices to family members or apprentices, for instance through apprenticeship programmes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One suggestion, I hope the Government will seriously consider, is for its programmes to be consolidated under a single, independent hawker academy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was a suggestion mentioned in a related Adjournment Motion by my former colleague, Mr Leon Perera, in 2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such a focal point for the hawker trade could provide more tailored support for hawkers, as well as streamline the role of the Government in its support for the hawker ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, the culinary and entrepreneurial skills of a hawker are not learnt the way one would learn a more academic subject.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, I would like to make a specific call for the rule allowing only citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs) to work in hawker centres to be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a long-standing challenge faced by hawkers I talked to and represents a policy inconsistency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Sengkang Grand Mall, for example, Buangkok Hawker Centre is, as the name suggests, a hawker centre but for any other CapitaLand mall, this would be a food court and subject to a different set of rules. "What's in a name?", one might ask.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I wonder how effective this would be, given that the LTVP is not intended for long-term employment purposes at all and we are looking at, potentially, a limited pool of workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As stated on the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) website, the LTVP is for common-law spouses, step-children or handicapped children of an eligible Employment Pass or S Pass holders and parents of those earning over $12,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The move to allow the hiring of work pass holders would benefit hawkers who find it difficult to open their stall every day at full hours, and these are also likely the hawkers who have been toiling in the most challenging of conditions day and night for decades and many are likely to be one of our most loved hawker stalls with recipes that have withstood the test of time in a challenging F&B industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, many restaurants, coffee shops and food courts offering Singaporean cuisine rely partly on foreign labour to meet manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, I hope the Government can take proactive and concrete steps to address the business costs for hawkers, address the cost of living for Singaporeans and lastly, to revitalise the industry we Singaporeans love the most – our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Given the evolution of this business and the challenges ahead, we would need to assist these hawkers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are several initiatives already implemented by the Government to help existing hawkers better cope with the labour shortage.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They can hire family members who will be more willing to work long hours and are more committed to help sustain the business.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is definitely not easy to sustain and grow our hawker culture in this rapidly changing environment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Nevertheless, I believe the hawker culture is an important part of our cultural heritage and more must be done.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) had made a commendable effort in December 2020 for Singapore’s rich and vibrant hawker culture to be recognised in the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)

text: The Hawkers' Development Programme, which trains and mentors potential hawkers, was launched by NEA in 2020.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In 2022, the Hawkers Succession Scheme was launched, to help retiring veteran hawkers pass their culinary skills, recipes and hawker stalls to aspiring successors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, the take-up rate for these schemes to establish a more systematic framework to attract and develop aspiring hawkers is still low to date.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to push harder in order to entice young hawkers into the trade with more creative incentives. : Mr Speaker, Sir, I have two suggestions for NEA's consideration.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The first is to organise a grand annual competition and provide credible recognition to outstanding hawkers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Such features and awards can help raise awareness that being a hawker requires a special distinguished craft, just like how a Michelin chef is recognised.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The competition can include various categories, showcasing preservation of traditional techniques and heritage dishes, creativity in new recipes, healthier food selections, excellence within cost constraints or excellence within slightly higher budgets, to cater to different taste buds and different pocket sizes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This reward could be a pragmatic way to encourage talented young people to enter the hawker profession as it enables them to start off with an advantage.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One way is to form a panel to identify and promote certain local brands and assist them to look into pre-packaged meals for the retail market.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They can either be dried, canned or frozen.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With new ideas and creativity, we can further strengthen Singapore’s local hawker brand names and, in turn, raise awareness for our hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our Singaporean food culture is about our good and affordable hawker food and this is a gem that must continue to shine.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I support the amended Motion put forth by Member Mr Edward Chia.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, I serve as a member on the National Heritage Board.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I am also currently Vice President of the Restaurant Association of Singapore and also Executive Chairman of a food service business.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hawkers play a key role in the F&B landscape.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: They continue to provide tasty and affordable meals for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hawker food continues to remain largely affordable owing to a variety of factors.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In F&B, the three main cost components are cost of space, that is, rental; cost of food, that is, the raw materials that go into the dish; and manpower.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, an F&B business thrives or survives when it generates sufficient revenue to cover all operating expenses.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Government policy thus far has recognised the value and place of hawkers in our society, and it would seem the majority of hawkers benefit from generally low and manageable rentals in the 100-plus hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, on the issue of rents, can there be a better way to support hawkers moving forward?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Recent high bids in popular centres have raised the question of whether the bidding system is still the correct approach.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at the hawker centres, in many hawker centres there will be a few stalls with long queues and many where we can just walk up and order.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It is the same pattern in other F&B concepts, whether these are food courts, quick service restaurants or full service restaurants.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some will have waiting lines, while others, you can be seated almost immediately.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are also variations in revenue levels for the same concept over various geographical locations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: So, one particular brand in one particular location may attract a certain level of revenue and be different in another location.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some malls, where the foot traffic is high, the F&B outlets located there enjoy proportionately stronger sales.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But this comes at a cost – higher rents.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In the case of private landlords, private landlords set the rental and the tenant decides whether to accept it or not or negotiate over the best available rental.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In Government hawker centres, the potential tenant offers the landlord what is considered affordable.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: A seasoned or experienced hawker will know the potential of the business and would have done the maths on what to bid and what is affordable.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The alternative to the bidding system would be a balloting system where the rent is fixed and the variable then becomes the luck of the draw.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, feel the Government is addressing the issue of rental costs at hawker centres in a reasonable and fair manner under the current circumstances.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The next big cost item for all food businesses is cost of raw materials.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, we have seen food costs escalate, owing mostly to external factors.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Inflation and higher costs have impacted many industry sectors, not just the F&B sector.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, higher food costs would naturally hit us more noticeably and directly.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Typically, a business will raise selling price to retain operating margins.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, for F&B, this is often not so clear-cut.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We are truly spoilt for choice in F&B.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, operators, myself included, would need to be judicious in raising selling prices.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The similar cautious approach is taken by hawkers who are concerned that a price increase will result in loss of customers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Recent reports suggest that many hawkers prefer to accept the lower operating margins rather than risk losing business through a price increase.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some suggest that public perception of hawker food is low price and hence, this makes it more difficult for customers to accept price increases.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The discerning customer will make choices, weighing price, quality, convenience and a variety of other factors.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are many initiatives to raise the profile of hawker food, with the intention to get the general public to accept paying more for hawker meals.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It should be noted though that there are some hawkers who do not intend to raise prices.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some feel that they want to keep the meal affordable for those who would be adversely affected by price increases.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Others would feel that they have comfortable earnings even though margins are down.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In this cost area, the Government has been managing inflation at the macro level and, as mentioned by hon Members earlier, provided supplementary efforts, such as the CDC Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The CDC Voucher scheme has the dual impact of helping households meet higher rising costs and supporting spending at selected merchants, including hawkers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The third cost component, manpower, is a continuing challenge for the F&B sector.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While some hawkers work as a family unit, there are those who will need to hire assistants and the cost of this has increased.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the issue of supply of manpower.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Manpower costs are not as key a cost component for hawkers as other F&B concepts.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But where margins are challenged, any increment eats into the bottom line.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Consumer spending does flow with the economic tide.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: During better times, it is possible that consumers will be willing to spend more on F&B and, therefore, replace a hawker meal with one at a higher cost option.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, when we need to tighten our belts, the demand for hawker food may well increase.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I believe these will be constantly reviewed and enhanced, where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The support during and post-COVID-19 would have brought welcome relief to many hawkers, though some hawkers will have been impacted more negatively than others.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While some hawkers have moved into second and third generations, many cease operations when there is no opportunity for succession.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: F&B operators have been seizing the business opportunity for some popular stalls and scaling these to multi-outlet operations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It remains to be seen how this will feed into the continuity of our hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are also examples of hawkers who have grown into full scale restaurants on their own and not just one restaurant, but several outlets.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hawker culture as we know it will need to evolve.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The case study, entitled "Cooking or Cooked: The Future of Singapore's Hawker Culture" by Khor Jia Wei and Kenneth Tan, helpfully lists the multiple issues and factors feeding into the sustainability of the hawker industry.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Public policy is just one of the factors.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As we reframe our definition of success, there may well be a rethink on where providing good and affordable food, or taking on a thriving hawker business into the next generation will be on this list.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The perfect opportunity came in 2011, when Minister Vivian Balakrishnan became the Minister for Environment and Water Resources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My arguments then were, firstly, coffee shops were changing hands at very high prices at the time, in the tens of millions, which had direct flow-on effects on stall rentals and added upward pressures on food prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There was a need for the Government to intervene, so that the mass retail food market would continue to be affordable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The inadequate supply of affordable hawker spaces then would be a major impediment to would-be hawkers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, we needed to tackle the insufficient supply of hawker stalls.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My third argument then was, it may not be intended that way at its inception, but today's hawker centres have become our unique social melting pot.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is huge social value in having a publicly-run, not-for-profit common eating spaces, where people from all walks of life can come together, under one roof to dine.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Upon completing the relocation exercise in around the mid-1980s, the Government stopped building new hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And the reason is that the Government felt that the provision of eating places and food can be left to the private sector, such as coffee shops and food courts business operators.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is good reason for that, a good position to begin at that time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Indeed, the Government should not be the sole or dominant retail F&B space provider and manager.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The private sector can and should have a role in this F&B ecosystem and besides, the Government also need to focus on its role as a regulator too.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, what happened around 2011 and prior was that the market mechanism had not worked out in the way as intended.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Coffee shops and food court spaces were traded at bubbly high prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It would have direct bearing on the stall rentals and thereafter, the cooked food prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This would not be sustainable to the hawker trade and would impact the overall affordability of cooked food prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, my point here is that, while we leave it to market forces to sort out most of the things, there can be situations where the market forces can bring us to the wrong place, such as runaway coffee shop prices, unhealthy market power and monopolistic behavior by dominant players, or that where coffee shops or retail F&B spaces have become speculative assets for trading.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is a need for the Government to intervene by way of supplying more hawker spaces then to stabilise the markets, no different from how the Government intervene to manage, say, our currency, the Singapore dollar, to keep within a trading band or the cooling measures to tame the hot property markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hawker centres are relatively low capital expenditure infrastructures, they are mostly non-air conditioned and built with a pretty unsophisticated design deliberately, with the purpose to keep maintenance costs low.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Because of the typically large floor spaces, it can accommodate more stalls under one roof and offer a wide selection of food choices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a result, hawker centres are a more competitive marketplace, which helps keep prices of food in check.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But after some wait, I finally have one at my then-constituency, in the Senja area.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And that is how we entered the new era of hawker centres development.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would call this the Hawker Centres 2.0, where a new generation of modern hawker centres sprouted up across the island.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While I am glad that the Government has decided to resume building hawker centres and giving the hawker trade a new boost in life, we also know that it comes with both new and old challenges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our first-generation and even second-generation hawkers are catching up in age.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is understandable that the younger generation may not see hawker trade as their first career choice, although I have also met quite a number of younger ones as well, including at Bukit Panjang.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Walter Tay is one of them and he runs "Father and Son Carrot Cake".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is also the Hawkers' Development Programme, which helps to equip aspiring and existing hawkers with the relevant skills and competencies to run a hawker business.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have to keep reviewing these programmes to see if it achieves the intended outcomes and if need be, to introduce new schemes to encourage new hawkers to join the trade.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many enter the trade as a calling and because of their passion for culinary and local food culture.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should show appreciations and cheer them on, including their stall assistants and the cleaners and the dishwashers at the hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hawker cooked food businesses are labour intensive work.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The number of meals served and how long is the stall opening hours are, are dependent on the number of stall assistants available at the stalls.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These days, it is difficult to find local stall assistants.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among the reasons, the work at hawker centres is physically demanding and the work environment not so appealing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The policy position has always been that hawker stallholders should be reserved for Singaporeans and PRs, to safeguard the local identity of our hawker culture.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope that can, in some way, alleviate the manpower situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, the other aspect to help hawkers improve productivity is also important.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I understand that hawker centres have tapped the various productivity support programmes, such as the Productive Hawker Centres programme, to enjoy the 70% tiered subsidies for centralised dishwashing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are also other bulk-purchasing services initiatives to reduce the toil on the workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having a larger pool of available stall assistants and to continue to work on improving productivity hopefully can move the needle and alleviate the situation faced by the hawkers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The third challenge is about the rising input costs and the food price tensions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hawkers, like all of us, wants a decent wage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, how do we achieve both and where is the balance?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Indeed, prices of cooked food have risen in the last few years, primarily due to rising input costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Raw food ingredients among the key components, which are pricier today due to higher global food commodity prices, the extreme weather also has an impact, and the knock-on effects from the higher energy and transport costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the weekend, I had a chat with Mr Ong Chye Lai, who runs the popular lor mee stall at Bukit Panjang Hawker Centre, to validate NEA's numbers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And he shared with me that, indeed, a major bulk of the cost increases come from his ingredients, such as the fish and meat that he serves, as well as the spices for his lor mee.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: He added that post-COVID-19, the prices of these ingredients have fluctuated at a wider range and he is trying to cope with the volatility.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How do we fight rising prices that are externally driven, such as supply chain disruptions, the war in Ukraine, the weather, the volatility in the global food commodity markets and that we import almost all of these inputs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, in the case of Singapore, we have some very helpful levers to mitigate the impact to our domestic economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Most of what we consume are imported and if our Singapore dollar is weak, it will be a double whammy to everyone of us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know that a strong Singapore dollar is not a given and should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Markets have to see the value in the Singapore dollar, on the basis of fundamentals – do we have a strong and sound economy, are we a strong and cohesive society and how are we as a country?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, it is also important to work on the other side of the equation as well, which is income.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to keep on working on income to rise so that it can help us mitigate inflation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And here, again, we need to keep our economy strong and attract investments so as to keep having good jobs and incomes for our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The third lever is that we must always have a competitive, efficient and vibrant business ecosystem, where consumers have choices as to where they want to consume.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A consumer must have a choice of at least three places to go to consume so that there is always competition.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A competitive business landscape helps keep costs and prices in check and help eradicate potential profiteering.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fourthly, there is the need for the Government to continue to give direct assistance to help Singaporeans cope with the rising costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And we do have a whole range of assistance schemes like GST Vouchers, U-Save vouchers, service and conservancy charges rebates, the Cost of Living payouts, CDC Vouchers, Workfare, Silver Support and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some of these assistance measures are permanent in nature and adds up to the billions of dollars from our Budget allocation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Again, we are fortunate to be in this good fiscal position to help Singaporeans households directly and very extensively, to directly assist Singaporean households to cope with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The fifth lever is everyone of us – the community support initiatives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know in various constituencies, we all do have our ground-up initiatives to help our fellow residents cope with cost of living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, at Bukit Panjang Town, we have what we call the monthly "$1 Deal" initiative, "一元为定", to help reduce the impact of cost of living to our fellow residents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We use funding from the community or from donors and not imposing it on the stallholders or hawkers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are also the private sector initiatives in the neigbourhood such as DBS’ "5 Million Hawker Meals" scheme and the various grocery support schemes such as by Hao Ren Hao Shi, "好人好事", New Life Community Service and also organisations like the Association of Banks of Singapore who bring volunteers and offer groceries to our residents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Out-of-the-norm high rentals do attract a lot of attention and may influence future would-be stall bidders to bid higher and thereby, push up overall average rentals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, we need to figure out how we can prevent that from happening.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Let us keep a close watch in the subsequent biddings whether the change has any effect in discouraging outlier bids.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I also welcome NEA move to make available more information and make available the online business cost estimation tool to help tenderers make more informed and realistic bids.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having said that I would still want to come back to my suggestion that I raised in last month's Sitting, which is that besides tender price, we should also look at the quality of the bid or what we call the price-quality method, or PQM.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In that way, we can remove some of these unrealistic bids and reduce the incidence of outliers in the rental bid price.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We now see really modernised hawker centres, better facilities, better ambience – this is a good thing for the hawkers ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides the various support schemes to support individual hawkers, there is also the Hawker Centre Upgrading Programme to upgrade older hawker centres, there is the Toilet Improvement Programme which the Ulu Pandan Hawker Centre just recently benefited from, and there are the CDC Vouchers to support hawkers as well as heartland digitalisation packages to help support the overall hawker centre ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, there will continue to be challenges to the hawker trade, but as Mr Edward Chia stated in his amended Motion, we must continue to support our hawkers by regularly reviewing the policies and to sustain our hawker ecosystem, so that both the hawkers can earn a fair livelihood and Singaporeans at large can enjoy good and affordable hawker food.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Rushing to the scene, I found the wet market and an adjacent eating house completely destroyed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Another nearby coffee shop was also severely damaged and would remain closed for months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Immediately, we rallied our volunteers to support the affected hawkers, who were devastated by the loss of their businesses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I reached out to NEA for a list of alternative cooked food stalls and market stalls at nearby hawker centres in the West, offering the hawkers a temporary place to continue their livelihoods while we began to explore options for rebuilding.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After consulting with the hawkers, nearby residents, volunteers, construction experts and the Government agencies, we chose to go ahead with a temporary market for several reasons.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Lastly, we saw an opportunity not just to restore what was lost but to create something better for the hawkers, the community and the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The reason we were able to build the temporary market in just six weeks, instead of six months, was the unwavering commitment of the entire Government to support the hawkers during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This extraordinary achievement would not have been possible without the dedication and collaboration of our partners.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I want to express my heartfelt thanks to the donors, HDB, NEA, the Public Utilities Board (PUB), the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) and all the Government agencies whose collective effort made this a reality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: During this period, from 2016 to 2018, my team and I effectively became the developers and operators of the temporary market.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We gained a deeper understanding of the hawkers’ challenges and the nuances of operating a hawker stall.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I recall that when we first provided the list of available stalls managed by NEA to the cooked food stallholders affected by the fire, their initial concern was rental rates.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When they learned that some stalls could be rented for as low as $1 per month, they were immediately skeptical.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The hawkers were forthright, expressing that while rental rates were important, their primary concern was foot traffic and community reach.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The experience of managing a temporary market and overseeing the rebuilding of a new market and eating house proved to be invaluable when I later worked with the NEA to reopen the Jurong West Hawker Centre in West Coast GRC.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The old Jurong West Market and Hawker Centre faced significant challenges to stay afloat, battling fierce competition from a nearby food court and a 24-hour supermarket.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The isolated location of its cooked food stalls on the second level, hidden away from the public eye at street level, gave them more challenges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To ensure the success of the new centre, we conducted a survey of over 2,000 nearby residents to better understand their preferences for wet market stalls, cooked food stalls, or a combination of both.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The results revealed that more residents preferred a combination of both.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, when we examined the responses more closely, we found that many of those who expressed a preference for wet market stalls had rarely, if ever, shopped there.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And some had visited only once in a blue moon.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This insight gave us valuable perspective on the real needs and habits of the community.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Today, the revitalised Jurong West Hawker Centre is doing much better than before.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The tenants pay a fixed rental fee to the SEHC operator of the Jurong West Hawker Centre, Chang Cheng, rather than through a price bidding system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The tenants also received rental discounts in the first couple of years of operations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The operator organises fringe activities periodically to bring in the crowd and plans to offer discount vouchers to vulnerable families.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, many of us have local schemes to help our residents better cope with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In Nanyang division, for example, blue CHAS card holders can apply for multiple $1 breakfast voucher to exchange for a $3 breakfast set from two main coffee shops at Blocks 815 and 959 Jurong West.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At Ayer Rajah-Gek Poh, low income residents receive $50 WeCare vouchers monthly to spend at local shops, including local hawker centre.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The above experiences underscore the Government’s steadfast support for our hawkers as well as our support to our vulnerable residents, to mitigate the impact from rising food costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The very concept of hawker centres was championed by the PAP Government and today, Singapore’s hawker culture is recognised on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But we continue to listen, adapt and improve to support our hawkers and Singaporeans who are patrons of the hawker centre.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Faced with this sudden incident, I immediately gathered grassroots leaders, volunteers and affected stallholders to engage in urgent consultations with relevant agencies, such as HDB and NEA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We decided to quickly set up a temporary market for the stallholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The smooth completion of this project was due to the full support from HDB, NEA, SCDF, PUB and other Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we also received donations from many kind-hearted individuals which enabled the temporary market to be completed so quickly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Between 2016 and 2018, my team and I not only had to operate the temporary market, but also prepare for the construction of the new market and food court.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This process was full of challenges and complexities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, it was precisely this experience that gave us a deeper understanding of the hard work and difficulties faced by hawkers in their daily operations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This valuable experience was very helpful later when I joined the West Coast GRC to assist NEA in planning the re-opening of the Jurong West Hawker Centre.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The new Jurong West Hawker Centre has been operating for over a year now, attracting a noticeably increased footfall, making it more convenient for everyone to enjoy good food.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These two examples fully demonstrate the joint efforts of the Government and civil society in improving the environment for hawkers and enhancing the diversity of our local cuisine.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, the tripartite partners have been working tirelessly to ensure that Singaporeans can enjoy high quality and more diverse local food. : Mr Speaker, Sir, the examples cited above showcase our continuous support for our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I fully support the Motion as amended by Mr Edward Chia.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hawker culture, recognised by UNESCO as part of our intangible cultural heritage, is not just about food.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about a way of life that brings together Singaporeans from all walks of life, around the humble dining table of our hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In recent years, we have the Singapore Government, including MSE and NEA, stepping up significantly to support and preserve hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, for instance, the Government implemented several measures to protect hawkers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Rental and table-cleaning waivers and salary subsidies through the Jobs Support Scheme were granted to ease the financial strain during these uncertain times.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: CDC Vouchers were also introduced to encourage locals to support their neighbourhood hawkers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These initiatives were designed to help hawkers sustain their livelihoods through challenging times, such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Policies aimed to sustain the hawking industry were introduced.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, big thanks to the Ministers for Finance – then, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat and now, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A unique feature in the safety net, the CDC Voucher scheme has the dual purpose of supporting both Singaporeans and the heartland businesses, especially hawkers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Infrastructure improvements are another critical element of preserving hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, NEA has initiated several programmes to modernise and maintain hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: NEA-managed hawker centres have seen substantial upgrades in facilities, cleanliness and ventilation, ensuring that patrons can enjoy a pleasant dining experience.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are essential to the continuity of hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A clean, safe and well-ventilated environment encourages patrons to return and also helps retain hawkers to stay on in their trade and jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides social enterprises which manage hawker centres, the Town Councils also manage hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: NEA, with its resources and expertise, has been able to uphold high operational standards in the NEA-managed hawker centres, whereas the Town Councils face some limitations, due to their smaller budgets and also fewer specialised resources, as they were primarily set up to serve residential estates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Town Councils primarily rely on S&CCs from stallholders, which are usually insufficient to cover the extensive maintenance costs required to match NEA standards.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This resource gap is particularly evident in our Central District hawker centres, such as People's Park Complex, Albert Centre and Chinatown Complex, which serve not only local residents but also a significant number of tourists.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: By doing so, NEA can apply its specialised expertise and substantial resources to ensure that these centres continue to reflect the high standards associated with Singapore's hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Alternatively, if taking over these iconic hawker centres is too daunting for now and actually needs further review, then I urge NEA to consider providing a resource package or support framework for these specific centres, acknowledging the unique demands placed on them as tourist hotspots and cultural icons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on the need to look beyond financial incentives to sustain and grow Singapore's hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hawking is also perceived to be a job that reaps modest income.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These root causes are not easy to solve and will take more than financial resources and incentives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Which ones should be managed by the State and which ones by Town Councils or social enterprises?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If the Government were to subsidise the costs of operating hawking businesses, especially in housing estates with predominantly Singapore residents, then can or should they reserve the right to at least control the rental and ensure budget meals for Singaporeans? "Budget meals" is not a dirty term.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are some of the questions that we have to and need to be reckoned with, as we review how to support and promote hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What has been made clear in the debate thus far is our collective passion for sustaining our hawker culture by ensuring that hawker centres remain affordable and accessible, helping hawkers address current operating challenges, such as the increasing cost of ingredients, the rising costs of running a stall and a manpower crunch.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We also need to put focus on attracting and empowering the next generation of hawkers to continue this tradition as ageing veterans retire, preserving our culinary heritage while innovating to meet evolving tastes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is also clear that the experiences of our hawkers are varied.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Different SEHC managers, different locations, different rental rates, different offerings and pricing strategies and, indeed, different hawker aspirations and expectations, lead to different experiences.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We can see the Government continuing to invest in new and upgrading hawker centre infrastructure and refining its policies to sustain our hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sometimes, the issue is not the policy, but the implementation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, improvements are probably needed in the operating processes and practices of specific SEHCs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, we could incorporate 360 feedback from customers and especially hawkers, to become inputs into PQM tenders and ongoing performance assessment of SEHCs, to help them improve.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: After all, hawkers are very important stakeholders in the ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will focus my speech on the community aspect of hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond the good and affordable food, our hawker centres have long been about community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Places where people from all walks of life come together with their friends and families, share stories, celebrate milestones – except perhaps a first date for Gen Zs, by the recent report – and enjoy our culinary heritage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As a Woodlands resident and third-generation hawker, Deen, observed, the veteran hawkers like his grandmother are the salt-and-earth people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Their fellow stallholders and their customers, whom they know by name, are their community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sure, sometimes, there would be disagreements between hawkers, especially when they sell the same type of food, but, generally, hawkers within a hawker centre get along.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They give back, too, as a community, to the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Deen shared how when a hawker wanted to give free meals to, say, a mosque, the whole row of stalls would chip in.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is their way of doing good while also gaining goodwill within the community and marketing their hawker centre and their own food.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even today, many of us have probably seen hawkers quietly dishing out meals to needy residents for only a few coins in return, without much fanfare, affording them dignity along with their food.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Given this community spirit, it is only right that beyond Government policies, beyond actions to be taken by NEA, SEHCs and other ecosystem players, we look to the wider community to be engaged in sustaining our hawker culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is much that we, as a community, can do to support hawkers while ensuring that anyone, regardless of their circumstances, can enjoy a good meal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Volunteers top up the available meals at each stall every week to ensure that residents always have a good selection.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: All of this is facilitated by a nifty little app built by volunteers in our Woodlands Digital Office.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This short summary belies the community spirit that underpins this programme.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our stallholders refer to us customers who they believe would benefit from the BAM programme.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We sign them up and also get them other help that they can benefit from beyond BAM.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They also tell me when their customers share with them their problems and encourage them to approach me for help at my Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many of our stallholders are regular contributors to BAM@Woodlands themselves, especially after a few big redemptions in a day can wipe out their balance of free meals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And the community has really rallied behind it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Mak Kai Chong, a regular donor donating $10 to $20 each time, wrote: "I want to contribute to my community and I find the BAM idea fantastic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If I have a little more than I need, I try to live kindness and care through action rather than being an observer." Yong Sit Lin, who donated $100, wrote: "I donated so that people in need can have a good meal." Marie Ong, who donated $1,000, wrote: “I always believe that to be able to help others in need or to create positive change is a beautiful thing!

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I love to see the smile on everyone’s faces and spread love and joy around.” Amalina Mutalib, who donated $10, wrote: “I donated because I know what it feels like to feel hunger.” An anonymous donor who donated $20 wrote: “I have the tendency to lose my wallet and forget where I put it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I found my wallet today and I take is as a sign that God wants me to donate!” Muhammad Faqih Karamy, who donated $10, simply wrote: “I sayang Sembawang.” Finally, an anonymous donor who wrote: “I like MP Mariam as I have been following her on Facebook and her projects have shown how much she cares for people, not just her constituents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Way to go, Ms Mariam!" I had to think twice about reading that last one out, but the point is really not to toot my own horn, but to share the insights, that Singaporeans care and are happy to help others enjoy good hawker meals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond the general public, we had great support from Northwest CDC to start it up, and corporate donors and patrons who made significant donations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In addition to helping our residents in need, BAM@Woodlands was a great help to our hawkers during the dark days of COVID-19 when business was low and continues to be a source of business today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It has also strengthened the bonds between hawkers and the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It was a splendid thought that I will make it happen for the Woodlands residents and make customers to be my new friends, and they supported me very well”.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In 2021, a stall assistant at Woodlands North Plaza met with a horrific car accident that left him in a coma for months and huge hospital bills.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not knowing where else to turn to, his colleagues spoke to our volunteers who had been engaging with them on BAM@Woodlands.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our volunteers helped them to set up a crowdfunding appeal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Two of our stallholders at Kampung Admiralty, Mr Peh and Ms Chen, have even become our patrons, contributing to our Building Fund for the upgrading of Woodlands Community Centre which, when opened, will serve our community for years to come.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Now in its fourth year, BAM is still growing and has been expanded to other parts of Sembawang GRC, including to my colleague Ms Poh Li San's ward in Sembawang West.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To me, BAM@Woodlands embodies the kampung spirit of our Woodlands Community at its finest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe we can do more to scale up such initiatives across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By working with local organisations, grassroots and hawkers themselves, we can launch programmes similar to Belanja-A-Meal in every constituency.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Imagine a network of hawker centres where every meal bought could contribute to someone else’s meal, where acts of kindness ripple outwards, creating a culture of giving, of mutual support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By expanding programmes like this, we, the community, can help ensure that our hawker centres continue to be vibrant, inclusive spaces that reflect the Singaporean spirit.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We all have our favourite hawker stalls where our families will come together to catch up and enjoy a good meal, sometimes going across the country.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When I was living overseas, every trip home meant through a list of our favourite hawker food, which included mee mamak at West Coast and satay at Haig Road.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We know it is not easy to be a hawker, with long hours and a less that comfortable work environment, always on your feet.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Hawkers today face many challenges – increasing cost of ingredients, increasing operating costs and manpower shortages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These younger hawkerpreneurs want to bring new ideas and concepts that cater to the evolving tastes of their customers and dream of expanding their business.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How many of us had our first taste of Western food at a hawker center?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One example is Mak’s Place, started by a Chinese Muslim couple.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Their story tells of how they saw a gap in the market for Halal Chinese food and started with a hawker stall in 1999.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: After two years, they started Mak’s Place, the hawkerant in Changi, selling the same good food at reasonable prices, in a more comfortable ambience with air conditioning, while giving back to the community in many ways, including providing free food to the less fortunate, providing jobs and mentoring to ex-offenders, and food and medical care to community cats.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many in our community want to follow in their foot steps.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They want more flexibility to experiment with their menus and to make it easier for them to scale and expand their footprint and team, when the concepts are successful – whether it is opening stalls in other hawker centres, opening a hawkerant, cafe or restaurant.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government has launched programmes to support our hawkers, including young hawkers, and has continuously reviewed its policies to do so.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we in the community can also do our part.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One of the sources of inspiration in our hawker culture is how it has united the community, fostering a spirit of togetherness and generosity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: People can buy extra meals to be given away at participating hawker stalls or make an online donation that we would then channel to the hawkers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This simple idea has been embraced by the community and continues to grow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have now launched BAM in other parts of Sembawang GRC.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It has also strengthened the bonds between our hawkers and our community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our hawkers regularly participate in our community initiatives, especially during festive occasions when everyone is always looking to do good and perform charitable works.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Low-income families were able to choose their favourite kuih during the Sinar Ramadan grocery distribution at our community store, Store@Woodlands.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Deen and his young team set up Begerack at Bukit Canberra Hawker Center.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They are a regular feature at our community events with their very popular putu piring.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Begerack sponsored free hair cuts by skilled barkers from Sleek & Trendy Cut, set up by Upu, an ex-offender, to get our low-income residents ready for Raya.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We can do more to scale up such initiatives like this across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To sustain and grow our hawker culture, we must take a holistic approach.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This includes Government support but also community initiatives and efforts to empower the next generation of hawkers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us not under-estimate what we, the community, can do.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will be speaking about the Government's policies to keep food affordable and enable hawkers to earn a living and fair income.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Before he does so, I would like to share how the Government has been supporting Singaporeans with cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This Government understands Singaporeans' concerns and anxieties about high prices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We have taken decisive action to help and will not hesitate to do more if necessary.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: First, the Government has taken actions to tackle inflation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: A big part of the inflation that we are facing has external causes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic and the wars in Europe and the Middle East have contributed to rising food, energy and transport prices globally.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The stronger the Singapore dollar meant that inflation did not reach the highs seen in other countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Inflation has now fallen significantly from its peak.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Hawker food inflation, fallen, compared to the earlier part of this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Overall, core inflation in 2024 is expected to continue to decrease and to drop further in 2025.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: MAS' monetary policy will continue to ensure the medium-term price stability.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Second, we have introduced a comprehensive package of measures to cushion the impact on households and enhanced it several times.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Even as inflation has moderated, we know that Singaporeans still feel the impact of higher prices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In particular, the Government has been giving out CDC Vouchers to Singaporean households every year since the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The number of participating hawkers has grown over time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Half of the CDC Vouchers can be spent at hawkers and heartland merchants.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This means that CDC Vouchers not only help Singaporean households with their cost of living, but also support our hawkers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The Assurance Package is on top of the permanent GST Voucher, or GSTV, scheme that already supports lower- and middle-income Singaporeans and households with daily living expenses, including food.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We introduced this scheme in 2012 and have enhanced it over the years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Most recently, we have increased the GSTV cash amount in 2023 so that eligible Singaporeans can receive up to $850 in cash each year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We also implemented a personal income tax rebate of 50% tax payable for the year of assessment 2024, capped at $200, so that the benefits go mostly to middle-income workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Ms Hazel Poa has proposed more help for vulnerable groups, such as food discounts and more CDC Vouchers for the lower-income.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In fact, this is what the Government has been doing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: A lower-income household with two young children will get about $6,500 and a retired elderly couple with no income will get about $12,400.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Over the years, we have continued to enhance our measures that provide more targeted support to those who are more in need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For example, in Budget 2024, the Government announced an increase in the quarterly Silver Support payments and an income threshold to qualify for support to provide more help to low-income seniors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: On top of the national schemes, the CDCs and grassroots organisations also have their own schemes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We have heard what hon Members Edward Chia, Liang Eng Hwa and Mariam Jaafar have highlighted and what they have done for their community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Third, the Government stands ready to do more to support Singaporeans, should it be necessary.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The Government will continue to monitor global conditions closely.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For example, an increase in geopolitical and trade tensions may lead to higher commodity prices and reverse the decline in imported costs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The broad-based support that we have provided over the past few years will help every family, but we recognise that there may be still gaps for some households.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For these households, we will continue to review and update our social support schemes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We are also heartened that many in society have come together to help with cost of living, especially for the more vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Importantly, we will continue to sustain real income growth for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We do this by creating good jobs for Singaporeans, we help them upgrade their skills and earn a higher pay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is a more sustainable way to manage price pressures by ensuring that our incomes grow faster than inflation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We cannot control external factors like wars or disruptions, but a stronger Singapore dollar has helped to keep inflation rates in Singapore lower than elsewhere.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We have rolled out significant and broad-based support measures over the past few years to help Singaporeans with higher cost of living.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We stand ready to do more to help Singaporeans if needed in a sustainable, fair and effective way, with more help to lower- and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The main subject of our discussion today is hawker centres and my colleague Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will be setting out the Government's approach to hawker centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, some speakers, including Mr Leong Mun Wai, made reference to the "Budget Meal" schemes in HDB coffee shops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Also, we know that HDB coffee shops are often mentioned together with hawker centres, although they are regulated differently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, I would like to take this opportunity to make a few points.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They are important social nodes in the community and provide a variety of cooked food options at similar price points to hawker centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: HDB plans for the provision of coffee shops and other commercial amenities in new HDB developments carefully to ensure that HDB residents have convenient access to cooked food options and other daily needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Most residents have access to commercial facilities, such as shops, food courts or coffee shops, within 400 metres of their homes, or an approximately five- to 10-minute walk.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: By planning for a good supply of coffee shops and other F&B options in every HDB town and estate, we ensure that residents have options to choose from.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The competition will also help to moderate cooked food prices overall.
